headlines.article_text: Harvard’s endowment jumps 27% with SpaceX as top holding Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Harvard University's endowment grew 27.1% in fiscal year 2026, the school announced Thursday. The return was powered by a $2.2 billion stake in SpaceX that Harvard revealed in a regulatory filing in the second quarter. The rise comes amid a push by President Donald Trump's administration to seek penalties against the 21,000-student school, and threaten to withhold funding over diversity commitments and other issues. Students walk on campus at Harvard University, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Nov. 19, 2025. Reba Saldanha | Reuters Harvard University's endowment grew 27.1% in fiscal year 2026, its strongest return in five years, the school said in its annual financial report released on Thursday. The endowment, which beat the S&P 500's 22.3% total return in the same period by 4.8 percentage points, now totals nearly $68 billion. The outperformance came amid actions by the Trump administration to penalize the school and withhold funding from the university. "While markets can easily take back what they give, that return will strengthen the endowment's capacity to support the University over time," Harvard's chief financial officer Ritu Kalra and treasurer Timothy Barakett wrote in the 49-page annual report. "The University deliberately smooths distributions so that operating support does not rise and fall with the markets. Strong investment returns therefore support Harvard's work gradually, through future distributions." The returns marked the best year for the endowment, managed by the Harvard Management Company, since 2021. Harvard's fiscal year ends on June 30. In its second-quarter 13F filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission , Harvard unveiled a $2.2 billion stake in Elon Musk's SpaceX rocket and satellite company. It marked the endowment's largest single holding by value, trailed by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company at just under $350 million. Harvard's financial picture, though, is undermined by moves by the federal government. Federally-sponsored research revenue declined 19.5% to $509 million in fiscal 2026. And starting in the current fiscal year, "endowment resources will face an additional constraint, with the federal excise tax on Harvard's net investment income rising nearly six-fold, from 1.4% to 8%," Kalra and Barakett wrote. "We estimate the higher rate will cost roughly $300 million a year." "[I]n a year of returns like this one," the federal excise tax "would be several times larger," they noted. President Alan Garber acknowledged such headwinds, but said in the report that Harvard can still succeed. "Together, we have the opportunity to set the University on a path to excellence that none of us can imagine today," he said. "Notwithstanding the challenges and uncertainty, this is a thrilling time to be part of a great American institution devoted to Veritas." headlines.article_text: KFC to switch from Pepsi to Coca-Cola in 2027 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points KFC is switching from PepsiCo to Coca-Cola as its beverage supplier for U.S. restaurants. The fried chicken chain has served Pepsi drinks ever since the food and beverage giant acquired KFC in 1986. KFC is trying to win back U.S. diners who have ditched its buckets for rivals like Chick-fil-A. In this article YUM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A view of a KFC restaurant in Vallejo, California. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday. Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals like Chick-fil-A or Popeyes. "This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us." Beverage cups stacked inside a Yum! Brands Inc. KFC restaurant in Shelbyville, Kentucky, U.S., on Friday, Jan. 29, 2021. Luke Sharrett | Bloomberg | Getty Images For many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, like McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options like refreshers or "dirty soda." Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks. KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said. Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets. For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands. It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway, the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. In this article AAPL CSCO NVDA AMZN MSFT PLTR META Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Construction continues on a new helipad on the South Lawn of the White House and the East Wing ballroom on Aug. 24, 2026, in Washington, DC. Andrew Harnik | Getty Images Technology giants Nvidia and Cisco have committed millions to President Donald Trump 's White House ballroom renovation project, CNBC confirmed on Thursday. Nvidia and Apple each pledged $25 million to the project, according to a report from The Washington Post . Those were among the largest donations on the list, which totaled more than $330 million. "As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests," a Nvidia spokesperson told CNBC. "We were proud to be able to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves all Americans and have said so publicly since the donation was made." Amazon , Palantir , ServiceNow , Meta Platforms and Microsoft also contributed in the millions, according to The Post. Microsoft and Meta declined to comment on the report. Cisco confirmed its $5 million donation. Amazon, Apple, HP Inc. , Micron , Palantir, Salesforce , ServiceNow and Vast Space, which were all listed as major donors in the report, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Post reported that the ballroom donations were sent through a nonprofit trust, and donors received a pledge form for donating to the "Donald J. Trump Ballroom." Lawmakers and experts have repeatedly called out donations to the project, requesting information on the private donors. Some have also raised concerns over the potential influence these commitments could have on policy decisions or any federal contract awards. Tech leaders have largely favored Trump's pro-business, light-touch approach to antitrust and regulation, and some companies have secured hundreds of millions in contracts through artificial intelligence infrastructure and defense deals during his second term. Tech leaders like Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have been regulars at state dinners and meetings in Washington, and were central figures at the White House AI luncheon on Sept. 29. The documents obtained by The Post showed 67 contributions above $10,000 as of late September. Read the full story from The Washington Post here . headlines.article_text: Tesla Roadster reveal: What to know about the delayed EV Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Tesla plans to reveal its next-generation Roadster from a SpaceX test site in Texas. CEO Elon Musk first debuted the Roadster refresh concept in 2017 but Tesla has since missed every targeted delivery date. Musk has promised fans a new Roadster with "rocket thrusters" that could "allow a Tesla to fly." In this article TSLA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Elon Musk, chief executive officer of Tesla Inc., during a state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping, not pictured, in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Annabelle Gordon | Bloomberg | Getty Images Tesla is planning to show off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday, almost a decade after Elon Musk's company started taking deposits for the electric sports car. The event will be livestreamed from a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, near Waco. It's expected to begin at 7:55 local time (8:55 ET). Tesla's original Roadster, designed and engineered by a team led by founding CEO Martin Eberhard, used a Lotus Elise chassis and was first delivered in 2008, selling for roughly $100,000 in small volumes until 2012. The next-generation Roadster is expected to be a high-end, low-volume model that relies on SpaceX technology, such as cold gas thrusters, to enable it to hover. Musk fanatics have been gearing up for the demonstration, expressing their excitement on social media, but the Roadster isn't likely to have any material financial impact on the company. Tesla reopened reservations for the refreshed Roadster in recent weeks, accepting $50,000 deposits from prospective buyers in the U.S., Canada and China. Executives are expected to disclose specific pricing, details and production targets. Musk first promoted the refreshed Roadster concept at an event in November 2017 , and the following June in a series of tweets. He wrote at that time, "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car." The engines would improve speed and braking, and may "even allow a Tesla to fly." Tesla started taking $50,000 deposits in 2017, but has since missed every targeted delivery date. As recently as last October, Musk was hyping a Roadster demo that he hoped would happen before the end of 2025. That didn't take place either. Musk's former friend and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman mocked the Tesla CEO in posts on X last year over the extreme delays, showing screenshots of his own reservation and refund requests. "I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays," Altman wrote. "But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait." Altman got his refund, and the two ended up in court over a separate matter earlier this year related to OpenAI's governance and ownership structure. Others have kept their reservations. Lawrence O'Connor, founder and CEO of Other World Computing in Austin, Texas, told CNBC he reserved a Founder's Edition of the new Roadster in November 2017, effectively giving the company what he called an "interest-free loan" of $250,000. O'Connor wrote in a message that he plans to attend Thursday's event and is "excited to see what has been 9 years in the making." According to filings with the Federal Aviation Administration, Tesla established a no-fly zone around the SpaceX facility where it plans to show off the vehicle. The company had to scrap a demo on Oct. 1 due to weather issues. Tesla is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday. headlines.article_text: AI stocks sell-off in global tech rout on AI funding worries Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Nvidia, AMD, Intel and Dell dropped on Thursday, as AI stocks across the globe continued to sell-off. Collectively, 20 of the most valuable global AI and semiconductor stocks have shed more than $1 trillion in value so far this week. The declines came as investors grew increasingly concerned that higher borrowing costs could weigh on the massive capital spending In this article 9984.T-JP TSM ASM-NL NVDA SKHY ASML CRWV INTC NOK Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:36 04:36 Dave Mazza: Memory stocks are in transition Squawk on the Street Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence trade sank on Thursday, continuing a global sell-off. Collectively, 20 of the most valuable global AI and semiconductor stocks have shed more than $1 trillion in value so far this week, as interest rate hikes, AI financing and intensifying competition weighed on sentiment. Nvidia fell about 2% while AMD sank more than 2% and Intel lost about 4%. Dell Technologies sank 9%. Micron shares whipsawed and were down marginally in the afternoon. Neoclouds also dropped on Thursday, though CoreWeave rebounded and was up nearly 5% in afternoon trading. Nebius was trading marginally lower and IREN was down about 3%. Shares in the neoclouds pared earlier losses after comments from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang seemed to settle fears in the AI trade. Huang told Bloomberg at an event in Stockholm, Sweden, that he didn't see a need for Nvidia to backstop CoreWeave and that, "Their cost of capital is actually decreasing." A sell-off in global technology hardware stocks also deepened across Asia and Europe on Thursday. South Korean chip giant SK Hynix plunged more than 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics fell 8.73%. Other South Korean chip-related stocks also came under pressure. LG Innotek sank 8.95%, Seoul Semiconductor shed 9.28% and Samsung SDI declined 6.26%. In Japan, technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 7.9%. Semiconductor testing equipment maker Advantest plunged almost 14%, while chipmaking equipment supplier Tokyo Electron lost 6.45%. Renesas Electronics declined 8%. Taiwan's TSMC , the world's largest contract chipmaker, fell 1.81%. Over in Europe, Dutch semiconductor giant ASML traded marginally lower, Infineon Technologies shed 5% and ASM International was down 7%. CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN stock chart. Why stocks are selling off The declines come as investors grow increasingly concerned that higher borrowing costs could weigh on the massive capital spending required to build out AI infrastructure, putting pressure on technology companies that have benefited from the AI investment boom. Concerns around global memory chip oversupply as early as 2029, as manufacturers ramp up production capacity to meet surging demand from artificial intelligence, also seem to be weighing down sentiment. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT , said over the weekend that it had made a breakthrough on a new architecture that could boost memory density by packing more data into a smaller space, signaling intensifying competition in the memory space. Elon Musk in an X post said China would be making "a LOT of RAM in 2028." Why this little known Chinese chipmaker has caused a global stock rout Chief executives of Broadcom and Intel, meanwhile, warned on Monday that financing could become a major headwind to the AI boom, with Broadcom's Hock Tan saying it could be bigger challenge to AI expansion than shortages of chips or electricity. The sell-off followed a bruising session on Wall Street Wednesday, where technology shares led broader market losses after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data fueled concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates further. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.88% to close at 26,692.87, while the S&P 500 shed 1.11% to end at 7,718.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.09%. watch now VIDEO 6:59 06:59 Kospi on track for weakest close since April as global AI sell-off deepens Squawk Box Europe Dan Ives, tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the latest sell-off in AI-related stocks reflects growing concerns over the cost of financing massive infrastructure projects as U.S. Treasury yields climb above 5%, but added that underlying demand for AI computing power remains robust. "Higher yields raise the cost of financing these builds, and investors are right to focus on balance sheets and contract structure, but rates are a financing question, not a demand question," Ives said in a note. The latest pullback presents a buying opportunity, Ives said, adding that the AI infrastructure boom remained in its early stages despite mounting concerns over funding costs. "What would change our view is a demand signal, not a rate signal," he said, pointing to potential cuts in hyperscaler capital expenditure plans, canceled contracts or falling GPU rental prices as warning signs. headlines.title: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: CoreWeave, Salesforce, Rocket Lab, Kimberly-Clark & more
headlines.summary: Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: CRWV, CRM, RKLB, KMB Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. Semiconductors — Chipmakers fell on Thursday, dragging the tech sector lower on the day. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) is heading for its eighth losing day, down 2% in the session. Shares of Nvidia lost nearly 2%, while shares of Advanced Micro Devices and Marvell Technology fell more than 3%. Software makers — Software companies were a bright spot within the tech sector, with the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) adding about 1%. Shares of Salesforce gained almost 4%, while shares of Adobe rose more than 3%. Oracle 's stock climbed 2%. Consumer staples — Shares of consumer staples companies rose as investors fled the tech sector for relative safety. Campbell's stock added about 5%, and shares of General Mills and Conagra Brands gained more than 3% each. FMC Corp — Shares tanked 32% after the chemical manufacturing company slashed its guidance for the third quarter. The company now sees revenue in a range between $65 million and $125 million, sharply below the FactSet consensus estimate of $868.5 million. "Q3 demand was weaker than we expected, driven by challenging market conditions and elevated levels of higher-priced FMC products held in inventory by certain channel customers, which are limiting product movement and replenishment demand," said CEO Pierre Brondeau in a statement . Intuit — Shares added 6% after the company behind TurboTax and QuickBooks software announced that it will acquire Sequence , a revenue management platform. Kimberly-Clark — The maker of Huggies diapers saw its stock gain about 4% after it issued preliminary third-quarter results that topped Wall Street's estimates. The company earned $1.70 per share, excluding certain items, on revenue of $4.13 billion. That compares to the FactSet consensus call for $1.58 per share and $4.09 billion. Berkshire Hathaway — Shares ticked up 0.4% and headed for an 11th consecutive winning day. On Wednesday, Italian tech conglomerate Bending Spoons announced that Berkshire made a $330 million investment into the company. That's in addition to Berkshire's $600 million infusion into the company in July when Bending Spoons debuted on the Nasdaq. The RealReal — Shares rose 11% after the online marketplace for designer clothes announcrd that it has obtained a $150 million term loan as well as a $25 million senior secured revolving credit facility. The RealReal will use the proceeds to refinance its 2029 senior secured notes. Marsh & McLennan — The insurer saw shares jump 5% on the back of top- and bottom-line beats for the third quarter. Marsh reported adjusted earnings of $2.03 per share on revenue of $6.86 billion, compared with the FactSet consensus of $1.97 per share and $6.64 billion. The advance led the SPDR Insurance ETF (KIE) 1% higher on the day. CoreWeave — Shares of the cloud infrastructure technology company fell for a second day, losing 2% on Thursday as investors worry that CoreWeave, along with other technology companies, are borrowing too much for an artificial intelligence build-out. Artificial Intelligence infrastructure plays Nebius Group and Iren also slid 5% and nearly 8%, respectively. Shares of Dell Technologies lost 8%, and shares of data storage company Everpure fell 6%. Rocket Lab — The space company's stock dropped 11% after it delayed the launch of its Neutron rocket to 2027. SK Hynix — Shares of the South Korea-based company slid 2% as investors are concerned over funding the artificial intelligence build-out. The drop also follows a 7.6% drop in the South Korean Kospi index overnight. Penske Automotive — Shares popped 8% after the transportation company said it would be taken private by Motown Acquisition Corp., an entity owned by Penske Corp. and Mitsui, for $212 per share in cash. The deal represents a nearly 9% premium to Wednesday's closing price of $194.79 per share. The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027. Walmart — Shares of the retailer popped more than 2% after Deutsche Bank upgraded the stock to buy from hold, citing a positive outlook for 2027. The bank expects incremental margins to improve and noted current inflation levels could help the company attract consumers. Crocs — The footwear company's stock rose 6% after Barclays upgraded Crocs to overweight from equal weight. Analyst Adrienne Yih cited the company's progress on product innovation and category expansion and its international business growth as factors for the upgrade. — CNBC's Fred Imbert, Tom Rotunno and Nick Wells contributed reporting
